claim: Loading of mRNA onto the ribosomal 43S pre-initiation complex (PIC) and its subsequent scanning require the removal of the secondary structure by RNA helicases such as eIF4A.
source: Loading of mRNA onto the ribosomal 43S pre-initiation complex (PIC) and its subsequent scanning require the removal of the secondary structure of the by RNA helicases such as eIF4A.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field of translation initiation, presented as background information.

claim: The ES6S region of the 48S-PIC constitutes an extended binding channel for eIF4A-mediated unwinding of mRNA and scanning.
source: Here, we found that the ES6S region of the 48S-PIC constitutes an extended binding channel for eIF4A-mediated unwinding of mRNA and scanning.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including crosslinking experiments and functional assays.

claim: Blocking ES6S inhibited the cap-dependent translation of mRNAs that have structured 5′ UTRs (including G-quadruplexes).
source: Blocking ES6S inhibited the cap-dependent translation of mRNAs that have structured 5′ UTRs (including G-quadruplexes), many of which are involved in signal transduction and growth, but it did not affect IRES-driven translation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from oligonucleotide blocking experiments and translation assays.

claim: Many mRNAs with structured 5′ UTRs that are sensitive to ES6S blocking are involved in signal transduction and growth.
source: Blocking ES6S inhibited the cap-dependent translation of mRNAs that have structured 5′ UTRs (including G-quadruplexes), many of which are involved in signal transduction and growth, but it did not affect IRES-driven translation.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of the genome-wide translation data.

claim: Blocking ES6S did not affect IRES-driven translation.
source: Blocking ES6S inhibited the cap-dependent translation of mRNAs that have structured 5′ UTRs (including G-quadruplexes), many of which are involved in signal transduction and growth, but it did not affect IRES-driven translation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing minimal effects on HCV IRES and other IRES-driven viral mRNAs.

claim: Genome-wide analysis of mRNA translation revealed a great diversity in ES6S-mediated scanning dependency.
source: Genome-wide analysis of mRNA translation revealed a great diversity in ES6S-mediated scanning dependency.
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling and RNA-seq data showing variable sensitivity of different mRNAs to ES6S blockage.

claim: mRNA threading into the ES6S region makes scanning by 48S PIC slower but more processive.
source: Our data suggest that mRNA threading into the ES6S region makes scanning by 48S PIC slower but more processive.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on in vitro translation kinetics data and the differential effects of ES6S blockage on different mRNA types.

claim: Translation initiation of eukaryotic mRNA generally follows the scanning mechanism.
source: Translation initiation of eukaryotic mRNA generally follows the scanning mechanism, which starts with the attachment of an activated 40S ribosomal subunit (43S preinitiation complex; PIC) to the cap structure of mRNA (forming the 48S-PIC), and the movement of the resulting complex along the 5′ UTR of mRNA to locate the initiation codon (TIS, generally AUG).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of translation biology, cited from multiple references.

claim: The scanning mechanism starts with the attachment of an activated 40S ribosomal subunit (43S preinitiation complex; PIC) to the cap structure of mRNA (forming the 48S-PIC).
source: Translation initiation of eukaryotic mRNA generally follows the scanning mechanism, which starts with the attachment of an activated 40S ribosomal subunit (43S preinitiation complex; PIC) to the cap structure of mRNA (forming the 48S-PIC), and the movement of the resulting complex along the 5′ UTR of mRNA to locate the initiation codon (TIS, generally AUG).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The scanning process directly depends on the extent to which a particular mRNA recruits the PIC.
source: This process directly depends on the extent to which a particular mRNA recruits the PIC, but also on the degree of RNA secondary structure (classical dsRNA and G-quadruplexes) found in its 5′ UTR (Hinnebusch, 2011; Jackson et al., 2010; Kozak, 1989; Murat et al., 2018; Parsyan et al., 2011; Pelletier and Sonenberg, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The scanning process depends on the degree of RNA secondary structure (classical dsRNA and G-quadruplexes) found in the 5′ UTR.
source: This process directly depends on the extent to which a particular mRNA recruits the PIC, but also on the degree of RNA secondary structure (classical dsRNA and G-quadruplexes) found in its 5′ UTR (Hinnebusch, 2011; Jackson et al., 2010; Kozak, 1989; Murat et al., 2018; Parsyan et al., 2011; Pelletier and Sonenberg, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The 48S-PIC must inspect the mRNA sequence codon-by-codon in the decoding groove of 40S neck to locate the TIS.
source: To locate the TIS, the 48S-PIC must inspect the mRNA sequence codon-by-codon in the decoding groove of 40S neck (also known as the mRNA channel), which includes P and A sites for aminoacyl-tRNA binding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of translation initiation.

claim: mRNA molecules must enter the channel in a single-stranded form, which requires prior unwinding by the RNA helicases associated with the 48S-PIC.
source: Thus, mRNA molecules must enter the channel in a single-stranded form, which requires prior unwinding by the RNA helicases associated with the 48S-PIC.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the structural requirements of the decoding groove and established knowledge.

claim: eIF4A is the main helicase that removes local secondary structure by alternating cycles of binding and dissociation from the mRNA during the scanning process.
source: eIF4A is the main helicase that removes local secondary structure by alternating cycles of binding and dissociation from the mRNA during the scanning process (Parsyan et al., 2011; Rogers et al., 1999; Svitkin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: eIF4A binds eIF4G to form the eIF4F complex together with eIF4E.
source: eIF4A binds eIF4G to form the eIF4F complex together with eIF4E, which collectively promotes activation of the mRNA, recruitment of the PIC and the scanning process (García-García et al., 2015; Nielsen et al., 2011; Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002; Rogers et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The eIF4F complex collectively promotes activation of the mRNA, recruitment of the PIC and the scanning process.
source: eIF4A binds eIF4G to form the eIF4F complex together with eIF4E, which collectively promotes activation of the mRNA, recruitment of the PIC and the scanning process (García-García et al., 2015; Nielsen et al., 2011; Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002; Rogers et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other RNA helicases such as yeast Ded-1 (and perhaps its mammalian ortholog DDX-3), DHX-29, DHX-36 and DHX-9 have been reported to assist in the RNA unwinding and scanning of specific mRNA subsets.
source: Recently, other RNA helicases such as yeast Ded-1 (and perhaps its mammalian ortholog DDX-3), DHX-29, DHX-36 and DHX-9 have been reported to assist in the RNA unwinding and scanning of specific mRNA subsets (Gao et al., 2016; Guenther et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2018; Murat et al., 2018; Pisareva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: eIF4F binding to the cap removes the eventual secondary structure near the 5′ extreme of the mRNA (activation) to favor recruitment of the PIC.
source: It is thought that eIF4F binding to the cap removes the eventual secondary structure near the 5′ extreme of the mRNA (activation) to favor recruitment of the PIC.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on current understanding in the field.

claim: Recent data support the notion that mRNA is threaded into the channel from the solvent side of the 40S subunit through a chain of cooperative interactions involving eIF4E-eIF4G-eIF3-40S.
source: Recent data support the notion that mRNA is threaded into the channel from the solvent side of the 40S subunit through a chain of cooperative interactions involving eIF4E-eIF4G-eIF3-40S (Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: The scaffold protein eIF4G can bind both eIF3 (as part of the PIC) and the 40S subunit itself near the feet of the solvent side, thus promoting the attachment of PIC to mRNA.
source: The scaffold protein eIF4G can bind both eIF3 (as part of the PIC) and the 40S subunit itself near the feet of the solvent side, thus promoting the attachment of PIC to mRNA (LeFebvre et al., 2006; Villa et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Little is known about the topology of the 48S-PIC, in part because its presumably dynamic nature has limited the use of cryo-EM reconstruction.
source: However, little is known about the topology of the 48S-PIC, in part because its presumably dynamic nature has limited the use of cryo-EM reconstruction, which has successfully resolved more stable complexes including the PIC (Erzberger et al., 2014; Hashem et al., 2013; Marintchev et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The helicase eIF4A has been located bound to alphaviral mRNA on the solvent side of the 48S-PIC assembled in vitro.
source: Recently, the helicase eIF4A has been located bound to alphaviral mRNA on the solvent side of the 48S-PIC assembled in vitro (Toribio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A scanning complex model is supported in which eIF4A is placed at the leading edge of the 40S subunit, thus 'pulling' the complex forward as it advances along the mRNA.
source: This would support a scanning complex model in which eIF4A is placed at the leading edge of the 40S subunit, thus 'pulling' the complex forward as it advances along the mRNA (Marintchev et al., 2009; Toribio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous data, supported by citations.

claim: This model would explain the greater dependence on eIF4A activity of mRNAs that have structured or long 5′ UTRs, many of which are involved in cell-cycle regulation and proliferation.
source: This model would also explain the greater dependence on eIF4A activity of mRNAs that have structured or long 5′ UTRs, many of which are involved in cell-cycle regulation and proliferation (Modelska et al., 2015; Rubio et al., 2014; Wolfe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the model, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Natural inhibitors of eIF4A are currently being tested as anti-cancer drugs.
source: For this reason, natural inhibitors of eIF4A are currently being tested as anti-cancer drugs (Chu and Pelletier, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The existence of RNA extensions such as ES6S and ES3S protruding from the solvent side of the 40S body, specifically in mammals, has been interpreted as a platform to recruit eIFs and other ligands.
source: The existence of RNA extensions such as ES6S and ES3S protruding from the solvent side of the 40S body, specifically in mammals, has been interpreted as a platform to recruit eIFs and other ligands, as described recently for ES27L of the 60S subunit (Fujii et al., 2018; Knorr et al., 2019), although direct support for this idea has not yet been presented.
evidence: This is an interpretation from the literature, supported by citations, but noted as lacking direct support.

claim: Direct support for the idea that ES6S and ES3S serve as a platform to recruit eIFs and other ligands has not yet been presented.
source: The existence of RNA extensions such as ES6S and ES3S protruding from the solvent side of the 40S body, specifically in mammals, has been interpreted as a platform to recruit eIFs and other ligands, as described recently for ES27L of the 60S subunit (Fujii et al., 2018; Knorr et al., 2019), although direct support for this idea has not yet been presented.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of evidence in the field.

claim: The ES6S region is composed of four RNA helices near the feet of the 40S particle, which form a bundle of tentacle-like structures.
source: The ES6S region is composed of four RNA helices near the feet of the 40S particle, which form a bundle of tentacle-like structures (Anger et al., 2013; Lomakin and Steitz, 2013; Melnikov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is structural information supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two of the ES6S helices (ES6SA and ES6SB) project outward from the ribosome body.
source: Two of these helices (ES6SA and ES6SB) project outward from the ribosome body, and comparative analysis of the 40S particle alone and in PIC or 80S complexes suggested that these helices can undergo some degree of conformational change (Melnikov et al., 2012; Toribio et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is structural information supported by citations.

claim: Comparative analysis of the 40S particle alone and in PIC or 80S complexes suggested that ES6SA and ES6SB helices can undergo some degree of conformational change.
source: Two of these helices (ES6SA and ES6SB) project outward from the ribosome body, and comparative analysis of the 40S particle alone and in PIC or 80S complexes suggested that these helices can undergo some degree of conformational change (Melnikov et al., 2012; Toribio et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is an inference from comparative structural analysis, supported by citations.

claim: ES6S has been proposed to participate in the scanning process, at least for some viral mRNAs.
source: Moreover, because scanning is a unique capability of 40S that is not present in the bacterial 30S subunit, ES6S has been proposed to participate in the scanning process, at least for some viral mRNAs (Toribio et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a proposal from previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: The existence of a conserved pattern of ES6S rRNA sequence complementary with eukaryotic mRNA 5′ UTRs suggested a role for the ES6S region in mRNA loading onto PIC.
source: The existence of a conserved pattern of ES6S rRNA sequence complementary with eukaryotic mRNA 5′ UTRs also suggested a role for the ES6S region in mRNA loading onto PIC (Pánek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: The authors detected the interaction of AUG-downstream nucleotides of alphaviral mRNAs with the ES6S region of the 40S ribosomal subunit in previous studies.
source: In previous studies, we detected the interaction of AUG-downstream nucleotides of alphaviral mRNAs with the ES6S region of the 40S ribosomal subunit (Toribio et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a reference to previous experimental data by the authors.

claim: Alphaviral mRNAs contain a highly stable RNA stem-loop structure (DLP) located 27–31 nt downstream of the AUG.
source: These viral mRNAs contain a highly stable RNA stem-loop structure (DLP) located 27–31 nt downstream of the AUG, so we were able to snapshot the eIF4A helicase bound to mRNA in 48S PICs assembled in vitro.
evidence: This is a structural feature of alphaviral mRNAs, presented as established knowledge.

claim: The authors were able to snapshot the eIF4A helicase bound to mRNA in 48S PICs assembled in vitro using alphaviral mRNAs with the DLP structure.
source: These viral mRNAs contain a highly stable RNA stem-loop structure (DLP) located 27–31 nt downstream of the AUG, so we were able to snapshot the eIF4A helicase bound to mRNA in 48S PICs assembled in vitro.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about previous experimental work.

claim: The vast majority of specific crosslinking sites mapped to within the nt 700–910 region of 18S RNA, concentrating in the ES6SE (nt 865–910), ES6SC–D (nt 795–864), ES6SB (nt 740–793) and ES6SA (nt 681–735) helices.
source: The vast majority of specific crosslinking sites mapped to within the nt 700–910 region of 18S RNA, concentrating in the ES6SE (nt 865–910), ES6SC–D (nt 795–864), ES6SB (nt 740–793) and ES6SA (nt 681–735) helices (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from crosslinking experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: No crosslinking with the inner residues of 18S rRNA was detected, indicating that mRNA contacted only surface-exposed regions.
source: No crosslinking with the inner residues of 18S rRNA was detected, indicating that mRNA contacted only surface-exposed regions.
evidence: This is an inference from the crosslinking data.

claim: Abundant contacts were found not only with the projected parts of ES6S, but also with residues that are at the base of these helices (e.g. residues 802–803 of helix C), embedded in the protein–RNA layer of the 40S body.
source: We found abundant contacts not only with the projected parts of ES6S, but also with residues that are at the base of these helices (e.g. residues 802–803 of helix C), embedded in the protein–RNA layer of the 40S body (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a finding from the crosslinking data, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: An mRNA path through the ES6S region extends from ES6SE to the distal loop of ES6SC–D, including the ES6SB and ES6SA helices, and is flanked by ribosomal proteins such as eS7, eS4 and uS4.
source: This allowed us to draw an mRNA path through the ES6S region that extends from ES6SE to the distal loop of ES6SC–D, including the ES6SB and ES6SA helices, and that is flanked by ribosomal proteins such as eS7, eS4 and uS4 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the crosslinking data, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: SFV-DLP n27 mRNA generated a crosslinking pattern that is similar, though not identical, to that observed for unstructured mRNA.
source: SFV-DLP n27 mRNA generated a crosslinking pattern that is similar, though not identical, to that observed for unstructured mRNA.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative crosslinking experiments.

claim: The number of crosslinks to residues of the ES6SE and ES6SC-D helices increased in SFV-DLP n27 mRNA compared to unstructured mRNA.
source: Specifically, the number of crosslinks to residues of the ES6SE and ES6SC-D helices increased in SFV-DLP n27 mRNA compared to unstructured mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative crosslinking experiments, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: uS5 (formerly RPS2) was the hit with the highest score and coverage in proteomic analysis of RPSs that crosslinked with mRNA.
source: A similar pattern of crosslinked RPSs was observed for both mRNAs, with uS5 (formerly RPS2) the hit with the highest score and coverage (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from proteomic analysis, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Crosslinking of uS5 at +11 nt downstream of the AUG has been previously reported in 48S-PICs assembled in vitro using a synthetic mRNA and purified 40S subunits and eIFs.
source: Crosslinking of uS5 at +11 nt downstream of the AUG has been previously reported in 48S-PICs assembled in vitro using a synthetic mRNA and purified 40S subunits and eIFs (Pisarev et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a reference to previous literature.

claim: uS5 was localized between the mRNA entry channel and the ES6S region of the 40S subunit, extending about 48 Å along the channel.
source: Interestingly, uS5 was localized between the mRNA entry channel and the ES6S region of the 40S subunit, extending about 48 Å along the channel (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a structural observation based on the known structure of the 40S subunit, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Other crosslinked RPSs with lower scores were detected, including some located either on the solvent side of the 40S subunit (uS3, uS4, eS4, eS6 and eS24), or on the intersubunit side near the decoding site (eS19) and at the mRNA exit channel (uS17).
source: We also detected other crosslinked RPSs with lower scores, including some that were located either on the solvent side of the 40S subunit (uS3, uS4, eS4, eS6 and eS24), or on the intersubunit side near the decoding site (eS19) and at the mRNA exit channel (uS17).
evidence: This is a finding from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Both eIF4A and eIF3g could be crosslinked with alphaviral mRNAs bearing the DLP structure in previous reports.
source: In previous reports, we found that both eIF4A and eIF3g could be crosslinked with alphaviral mRNAs bearing the DLP structure (Toribio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a reference to previous work by the authors.

claim: Both eIF4A and eIF3g bands were crosslinked with SFV-DLP n27 mRNA to a similar extent.
source: Both eIF4A and eIF3g bands were crosslinked with SFV-DLP n27 mRNA to a similar extent, whereas unstructured mRNA generated strong crosslinking with eIF3g and little (if any) with eIF4A (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from crosslinking experiments, shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Unstructured mRNA generated strong crosslinking with eIF3g and little (if any) with eIF4A.
source: Both eIF4A and eIF3g bands were crosslinked with SFV-DLP n27 mRNA to a similar extent, whereas unstructured mRNA generated strong crosslinking with eIF3g and little (if any) with eIF4A (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from crosslinking experiments, shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The fact that unstructured mRNA generated no crosslinking with eIF4A is consistent with previous data showing the critical role of DLP structure in the trapping of eIF4A within the 48S-PIC.
source: The fact that unstructured mRNA generated no crosslinking with eIF4A is consistent with previous data showing the critical role of DLP structure in the trapping of eIF4A within the 48S-PIC (Toribio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference connecting current data with previous findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Maximum crosslinking with eIF3g was observed when 4-thio-U was placed +24 nt downstream of the AUG.
source: Maximum crosslinking with eIF3g was observed when 4-thio-U was placed +24 nt downstream of the AUG, whereas maximum crosslinking of eIF4A was achieved when 4-thio-U was placed at +27 nt.
evidence: This is a finding from systematic crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Maximum crosslinking of eIF4A was achieved when 4-thio-U was placed at +27 nt downstream of the AUG.
source: Maximum crosslinking with eIF3g was observed when 4-thio-U was placed +24 nt downstream of the AUG, whereas maximum crosslinking of eIF4A was achieved when 4-thio-U was placed at +27 nt.
evidence: This is a finding from systematic crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Crosslinking of eIF3g at position +24 fit well with the suggested placement of eIF3g bound to eIF3b near ES6SA.
source: By modeling mRNA placement throughout the ES6S region of the 48S-PIC (Toribio et al., 2018), we found that crosslinking of eIF3g at position +24 fit well with the suggested placement of eIF3g bound to eIF3b near ES6SA (des Georges et al., 2015; Eliseev et al., 2018; Hashem et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from modeling and comparison with previous structural data, supported by citations.

claim: According to the data, eIF4A may be placed a bit further downstream, probably between the ES6SA and ES6SB helices.
source: According to our data, eIF4A may be placed a bit further downstream, probably between the ES6SA and ES6SB helices (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is an inference from the crosslinking data and modeling, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Transfection of MEFs with VIC-oligo 4, but not with its unconjugated form, strongly inhibited protein synthesis at 12 hr post-transfection.
source: Transfection of MEFs with VIC-oligo 4, but not with its unconjugated form, strongly inhibited protein synthesis at 12 hr post-transfection (hpt) (Figure 3b, upper left panel).
evidence: This is a finding from metabolic labeling experiments, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Oligo 5.4 (both VIC-conjugated and unconjugated), which targets helix ES6SB, did not significantly affect translation.
source: In these experiments, we also included oligo 5.4 (both VIC-conjugated and unconjugated), which targets helix ES6SB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) without significantly affecting translation, showing that the effect of VIC-oligo 4 was specific.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating specificity, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of VIC-oligo 4 was specific.
source: In these experiments, we also included oligo 5.4 (both VIC-conjugated and unconjugated), which targets helix ES6SB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) without significantly affecting translation, showing that the effect of VIC-oligo 4 was specific.
evidence: This is an inference from the control experiment with oligo 5.4.

claim: A similar degree of translation inhibition was found for all of the fluorochromes tested (VIC, FITC, TR).
source: To test the role of the fluorochrome in the inhibitory activity of VIC-oligo 4, we replaced VIC with FITC or TR (Figure 3b, upper left panel), finding a similar degree of translation inhibition for all of the fluorochromes tested.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative experiments with different fluorochromes, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The inclusion of an additional mass at the 5′ end was responsible for the inhibitory activity of oligo 4 on translation.
source: This suggests that the inclusion of an additional mass at the 5′ end was responsible for the inhibitory activity of oligo 4 on translation.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that all fluorochrome-conjugated oligos had similar inhibitory effects.

claim: The effect of VIC-oligo 4 on translation was rapid, starting at 4–6 hpt and reaching a maximum at 8 hpt.
source: The effect of VIC-oligo 4 on translation was rapid, starting at 4–6 hpt and reaching a maximum at 8 hpt (Figure 3b, upper right panel), suggesting a direct impact on translation rather than an indirect consequence of cell growth arrest that was induced by VIC-oligo 4 some time after post-transfection (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course experiments, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The rapid effect of VIC-oligo 4 suggests a direct impact on translation rather than an indirect consequence of cell growth arrest.
source: The effect of VIC-oligo 4 on translation was rapid, starting at 4–6 hpt and reaching a maximum at 8 hpt (Figure 3b, upper right panel), suggesting a direct impact on translation rather than an indirect consequence of cell growth arrest that was induced by VIC-oligo 4 some time after post-transfection (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the time-course data.

claim: Analysis of polysome profiles at 6–8 hpt revealed the accumulation of 80S (monosomes) together with a decrease in heavy polysomes.
source: Analysis of polysome profiles at 6–8 hpt revealed the accumulation of 80S (monosomes) together with a decrease in heavy polysomes, strongly suggesting a blockade of the initiation step of protein synthesis (Figure 3b, lower panel).
evidence: This is a finding from polysome profiling experiments, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The polysome profile changes strongly suggest a blockade of the initiation step of protein synthesis.
source: Analysis of polysome profiles at 6–8 hpt revealed the accumulation of 80S (monosomes) together with a decrease in heavy polysomes, strongly suggesting a blockade of the initiation step of protein synthesis (Figure 3b, lower panel).
evidence: This is an inference from the polysome profiling data.

claim: No significant alteration in the 28S/18S ratio was detected at different times post-transfection.
source: We did not detect significant alteration in the 28S/18S ratio at different times post-transfection, nor alteration in the distribution of representative RPSs across the sucrose gradient, suggesting that 40S biogenesis was not significantly altered by the oligo (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: No alteration in the distribution of representative RPSs across the sucrose gradient was detected.
source: We did not detect significant alteration in the 28S/18S ratio at different times post-transfection, nor alteration in the distribution of representative RPSs across the sucrose gradient, suggesting that 40S biogenesis was not significantly altered by the oligo (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis of gradient fractions, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: 40S biogenesis was not significantly altered by the oligo.
source: We did not detect significant alteration in the 28S/18S ratio at different times post-transfection, nor alteration in the distribution of representative RPSs across the sucrose gradient, suggesting that 40S biogenesis was not significantly altered by the oligo (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA and protein distribution data.

claim: ES6S blockage by VIC–oligo 4 drastically reduced eIF4A/eIF3g crosslinking.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4, ES6S blockage by VIC–oligo 4 drastically reduced eIF4A/eIF3g crosslinking, suggesting that VIC–oligo 4 disturbed the interaction of mRNAs with ES6S region.
evidence: This is a finding from crosslinking experiments, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: VIC–oligo 4 disturbed the interaction of mRNAs with ES6S region.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4, ES6S blockage by VIC–oligo 4 drastically reduced eIF4A/eIF3g crosslinking, suggesting that VIC–oligo 4 disturbed the interaction of mRNAs with ES6S region.
evidence: This is an inference from the reduced crosslinking data.

claim: eS4–EGFP accumulated in the nucleolus and in the cytoplasm of transfected cells.
source: Overexpressed eS4–EGFP accumulated in the nucleolus, but also in the cytoplasm of transfected cells (Figure 3c, upper right panel), as previously reported for other overexpressed RPSs (Al-Jubran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from fluorescence microscopy, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: eS4–EGFP was incorporated into 40S and 80S particles with the same efficiency as eS4.
source: Comparison of the distribution of endogenous eS4 and eS4–EGFP in sucrose gradients confirmed that eS4–EGFP was incorporated into 40S and 80S particles with the same efficiency as eS4 (Figure 3c, lower panel).
evidence: This is a finding from sucrose gradient analysis, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: A differential increase in the 40S accumulation of eS4–EGFP was found when compared to that of endogenous eS4, suggesting a block in the pre-initiation step.
source: However, we found a differential increase in the 40S accumulation of eS4–EGFP when compared to that of endogenous eS4, suggesting a block in the pre-initiation step.
evidence: This is an inference from the sucrose gradient data.

claim: Protein synthesis was blocked by eS4–EGFP, to an extent comparable to that resulting from cycloheximide treatment.
source: Clearly, protein synthesis was blocked by eS4–EGFP, to an extent comparable to that resulting from cycloheximide treatment (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from OPP incorporation experiments, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: No significant differences in the distributions of the analyzed eIFs were found when eS4–EGFP was incorporated into the 40S particle.
source: To test whether the incorporation of eS4–EGFP into the 40S particle affected the binding of some eIF3 subunits (such as eIF3g, which binds eIF3b near ES6SA of 40S), we probed sucrose gradients with different antibodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), finding no significant differences in the distributions of the analyzed eIFs.
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis of gradient fractions, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: VIC–oligo 4 transfection reduced the accumulation of luc in all cases tested, but the extent of inhibition dramatically differed among the constructions tested.
source: VIC–oligo 4 transfection reduced the accumulation of luc in all cases, but the extent of inhibition dramatically differed among the constructions tested.
evidence: This is a finding from luciferase reporter assays.

claim: Translation of luc mRNAs bearing a long 5′ UTR (656 nt) or an average-sized 5′ UTR (121 nt) with a stable stem-loop structure (SL20) was dramatically impaired by VIC–oligo 4 transfection (50–80-fold inhibition).
source: Translation of luc mRNAs bearing a long 5′ UTR (656 nt) or an average-sized 5′ UTR (121 nt) with a stable stem-loop structure (SL20) was dramatically impaired by VIC–oligo 4 transfection (50–80-fold inhibition) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from luciferase reporter assays, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Translation of luc mRNA bearing a short 5′ UTR (33 nt) was much less affected by VIC–oligo 4 transfection (about two-fold inhibition).
source: By contrast, translation of luc mRNA bearing a short 5′ UTR (33 nt) was much less affected by VIC–oligo 4 transfection (about two-fold inhibition).
evidence: This is a finding from luciferase reporter assays.

claim: VIC–oligo 4 had only a modest effect (2–3 fold inhibition) on HCV IRES-driven translation, similar to that observed for mRNA with a short 5′ UTR.
source: We also tested the effect of VIC–oligo 4 on hepatitis C virus (HCV) IRES-driven translation, showing only a modest effect (2–3 fold inhibition), similar to that observed for mRNA with a short 5′ UTR (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from luciferase reporter assays, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Sensitivity to VIC–oligo-4-induced translational block increased with the 5′ UTR length of the mRNA.
source: We further confirmed that sensitivity to VIC–oligo-4-induced translational block increased with the 5′ UTR length of the mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from systematic analysis of mRNAs with different 5′ UTR lengths, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Accumulation of EMC or PV proteins was not significantly affected by VIC–oligo 4 transfection when compared with controls.
source: Accumulation of EMC or PV proteins was not significantly affected by VIC–oligo 4 transfection when compared with controls, whereas translation of SFV and VSV proteins was dramatically inhibited by VIC–oligo 4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from viral infection experiments, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Translation of SFV and VSV proteins was dramatically inhibited by VIC–oligo 4.
source: Accumulation of EMC or PV proteins was not significantly affected by VIC–oligo 4 transfection when compared with controls, whereas translation of SFV and VSV proteins was dramatically inhibited by VIC–oligo 4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from viral infection experiments, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: VIC–oligo 4 transfection of MEFs expressing the 5′ UTR ATF-4 Luc mRNA prevented the accumulation of luc upon thapsigargin treatment.
source: Clearly, VIC–oligo 4 transfection of MEFs expressing the 5′ UTR ATF-4 Luc mRNA prevented the accumulation of luc upon thapsigargin treatment, showing that VIC–oligo 4 did indeed block scanning and/or reinitiation on the 5′ UTR ATF-4 mRNA (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a finding from ATF-4 reporter assays, shown in Figure 4c.

claim: VIC–oligo 4 blocked scanning and/or reinitiation on the 5′ UTR ATF-4 mRNA.
source: Clearly, VIC–oligo 4 transfection of MEFs expressing the 5′ UTR ATF-4 Luc mRNA prevented the accumulation of luc upon thapsigargin treatment, showing that VIC–oligo 4 did indeed block scanning and/or reinitiation on the 5′ UTR ATF-4 mRNA (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is an inference from the ATF-4 reporter data.

claim: The sensitivity of transcriptome-wide mRNAs to VIC–oligo 4 varied more than 30-fold.
source: We found that the sensitivity of transcriptome-wide mRNAs to VIC–oligo 4 varied more than 30-fold, although the distribution of TE change was clearly skewed towards translation inhibition (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from genome-wide polysome profiling analysis, shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The distribution of TE change was clearly skewed towards translation inhibition.
source: We found that the sensitivity of transcriptome-wide mRNAs to VIC–oligo 4 varied more than 30-fold, although the distribution of TE change was clearly skewed towards translation inhibition (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from genome-wide polysome profiling analysis, shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Very small differences in total mRNA abundance were found when comparing cells transfected with oligo 4 and VIC–oligo 4.
source: Very small differences in total mRNA abundance were found when comparing cells transfected with oligo 4 and VIC–oligo 4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from RNA-seq analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'TE down' group was enriched in mRNAs that are involved in cell signaling and growth, especially in the G-protein-coupled receptor signaling and Ras pathways.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis revealed that the 'TE down' group was enriched in mRNAs that are involved in cell signaling and growth, especially in the G-protein-coupled receptor signaling and Ras pathways (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis, shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The 'TE down' group was enriched in KEGG pathway mRNAs related to cancer and other diseases.
source: This group was also enriched in KEGG pathway mRNAs related to cancer and other diseases (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from KEGG pathway analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'TE up' group was highly enriched in GO terms related to RNA metabolism, including mRNA splicing, rRNA processing and mRNA translation.
source: On the other hand, the 'TE up' group was highly enriched in GO terms related to RNA metabolism, including mRNA splicing, rRNA processing and mRNA translation (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis, shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The TE down group was enriched in mRNAs encoding membrane proteins and under-represented in mRNAs encoding nuclear proteins that have RNA binding or ligase activities.
source: Accordingly, the TE down group was enriched in mRNAs encoding membrane proteins and under-represented in mRNAs encoding nuclear proteins that have RNA binding or ligase activities (Figure 5b, lower panel).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis, shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The G+C content and the propensity to fold into secondary structures (RNAfold, ΔG°) were the 5′ UTR features that best correlated with TE groups.
source: We found that the G+C content and the propensity to fold into secondary structures (RNAfold, ΔG°) were the 5′ UTR features that best correlated with TE groups.
evidence: This is a finding from principal component analysis and feature comparison.

claim: 5′ UTRs of the 'TE down' group showed a higher G+C content than those of the 'TE up' group (74% vs 62.96%, p=3×10−49, U test).
source: 5′ UTRs of the 'TE down' group showed a higher G+C content than those of the 'TE up' group (74% vs 62.96%, p=3×10−49, U test), and a more stable predicted RNA secondary structure (−72.50 kcal.mol−1 vs −27.7 kcal.mol−1, p=3×10−23, U test) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of 5′ UTR features, shown in Figure 5c.

claim: 5′ UTRs of the 'TE down' group showed a more stable predicted RNA secondary structure (−72.50 kcal.mol−1 vs −27.7 kcal.mol−1, p=3×10−23, U test) than those of the 'TE up' group.
source: 5′ UTRs of the 'TE down' group showed a higher G+C content than those of the 'TE up' group (74% vs 62.96%, p=3×10−49, U test), and a more stable predicted RNA secondary structure (−72.50 kcal.mol−1 vs −27.7 kcal.mol−1, p=3×10−23, U test) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of 5′ UTR features, shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The 5′ UTRs of the 'TE down' group were larger than those of the 'TE up' group (p=6×10−12, U test).
source: The 5′ UTRs of the 'TE down' group were also larger than those of the 'TE up' group (p=6×10−12, U test) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of 5′ UTR features, shown in Figure 5c.

claim: A strong enrichment of 15-mer and 12-mer (GGC/A)4 motifs (E-value = 2.7×10−76 and 2.7 × 10−47, respectively) was found in the 'TE down' group.
source: Interestingly, we found a strong enrichment of 15-mer and 12-mer (GGC/A)4 motifs (E-value = 2.7×10−76 and 2.7 × 10−47, respectively) in the 'TE down' group that was not detected in the 'TE up' group (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from MEME motif analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: (GGC/A)4 motifs were not detected in the 'TE up' group.
source: Interestingly, we found a strong enrichment of 15-mer and 12-mer (GGC/A)4 motifs (E-value = 2.7×10−76 and 2.7 × 10−47, respectively) in the 'TE down' group that was not detected in the 'TE up' group (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from MEME motif analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A strong enrichment of the (G3N1–12)4 motif was found in the 5′ UTRs of the 'TE down' mRNAs (χ2 < 10−4), being 3-fold higher than that found in the 'TE up' group.
source: A strong enrichment of the (G3N1–12)4 motif was found in the 5′ UTRs of the 'TE down' mRNAs (χ2 < 10−4), being 3-fold higher than that found in the 'TE up' group.
evidence: This is a finding from G-quadruplex motif analysis using QuadBase2.

claim: About 75% of 'TE down' mRNAs contained either 12-mer (GGC/A)4 or classical G4.
source: About 75% of 'TE down' mRNAs contained either 12-mer (GGC/A)4 or classical G4 (Figure 5d, upper left panel).
evidence: This is a finding from motif analysis, shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The presence of G4 motifs rendered the translation of luc mRNA more sensitive to VIC–oligo 4.
source: Clearly, the presence of G4 motifs rendered the translation of luc mRNA more sensitive to VIC–oligo 4, whereas the presence of (GGC)4 had less of an effect.
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro translation experiments with reporter constructs.

claim: The presence of (GGC)4 had less of an effect on sensitivity to VIC–oligo 4 than G4 motifs.
source: Clearly, the presence of G4 motifs rendered the translation of luc mRNA more sensitive to VIC–oligo 4, whereas the presence of (GGC)4 had less of an effect.
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro translation experiments with reporter constructs.

claim: A correlation was found between the predicted stability of the G4 motif and the extent of translation inhibition by VIC–oligo 4.
source: Moreover, we found a correlation between the predicted stability of the G4 motif and the extent of translation inhibition by VIC–oligo 4 (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro translation experiments with different G4 variants, shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a dramatic reduction in the accumulation of CCND3, ODC-1, HRas and AKT1 protein upon VIC–oligo 4 transfection.
source: Western blot analysis revealed a dramatic reduction in the accumulation of CCND3, ODC-1, HRas and AKT1 protein upon VIC–oligo 4 transfection, whereas GRK2 protein accumulation was reduced but to a lesser extent (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: GRK2 protein accumulation was reduced but to a lesser extent than CCND3, ODC-1, HRas and AKT1 upon VIC–oligo 4 transfection.
source: Western blot analysis revealed a dramatic reduction in the accumulation of CCND3, ODC-1, HRas and AKT1 protein upon VIC–oligo 4 transfection, whereas GRK2 protein accumulation was reduced but to a lesser extent (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Time-course experiments confirmed the high sensitivity of CCND3, followed by AKT1 and HRAS, to VIC–oligo 4.
source: Time-course experiments confirmed the high sensitivity of CCND3, followed by AKT1 and HRAS, to VIC–oligo 4 (Figure 6b, right panel).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course western blot analysis, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The short half-life of the CCND3 protein (about 30 min) probably accounts for its rapid disappearance after blockage of de novo synthesis by VIC–oligo 4.
source: The short half-life of the CCND3 protein (about 30 min) probably accounts for its rapid disappearance after blockage of de novo synthesis by VIC–oligo 4.
evidence: This is an inference based on known protein stability and the observed kinetics.

claim: The accumulation of eIF4B increased slightly in cells transfected with fluorophore-conjugated oligo 4s, especially TR-oligo 4.
source: However, the accumulation of eIF4B increased slightly in cells transfected with fluorophore-conjugated oligo 4s, especially TR-oligo 4 (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis, shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Hipp, like VIC–oligo 4, reduced the accumulation of GRK2, AKT1 and CCND3 proteins.
source: Whereas hipp, like VIC–oligo 4, reduced the accumulation of GRK2, AKT1 and CCND3 proteins, HRAS translation was not affected by hipp, and translation of eIF4B mRNA increased upon treatment with hipp, as also observed for TR–oligo 4 (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative western blot analysis, shown in Figure 6c.

claim: HRAS translation was not affected by hipp.
source: Whereas hipp, like VIC–oligo 4, reduced the accumulation of GRK2, AKT1 and CCND3 proteins, HRAS translation was not affected by hipp, and translation of eIF4B mRNA increased upon treatment with hipp, as also observed for TR–oligo 4 (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis, shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Translation of eIF4B mRNA increased upon treatment with hipp, as also observed for TR–oligo 4.
source: Whereas hipp, like VIC–oligo 4, reduced the accumulation of GRK2, AKT1 and CCND3 proteins, HRAS translation was not affected by hipp, and translation of eIF4B mRNA increased upon treatment with hipp, as also observed for TR–oligo 4 (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis, shown in Figure 6c.

claim: These results suggest a partial functional overlap of the ES6S region and helicase eIF4A in the translation of specific mRNAs.
source: These results suggest a partial functional overlap of the ES6S region and helicase eIF4A in the translation of specific mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparative effects of VIC-oligo 4 and hippuristanol.

claim: Translation of eIF4A-dependent mRNAs was also affected by VIC–oligo 4.
source: Notably, translation of these eIF4A-dependent mRNAs was also affected by VIC–oligo 4, and about half of the eIF4A-dependent mRNAs fell into our VIC–oligo-4-sensitive group (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from comparison with published eIF4A-dependent mRNA datasets, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: About half of the eIF4A-dependent mRNAs fell into the VIC–oligo-4-sensitive group.
source: Notably, translation of these eIF4A-dependent mRNAs was also affected by VIC–oligo 4, and about half of the eIF4A-dependent mRNAs fell into our VIC–oligo-4-sensitive group (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from comparison with published datasets, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: ES6S blockage seems to have a wider impact on translation than eIF4A downregulation.
source: However, in comparing our data set with the available information on the genome-wide effects of eIF4A inhibition or downregulation, we find that ES6S blockage seems to have a wider impact on translation than eIF4A downregulation (Modelska et al., 2015; Rubio et al., 2014; Wolfe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from comparison with published datasets, supported by citations.

claim: Translation of AKT-1 mRNA was strongly inhibited by eS4–EGFP overexpression.
source: Notably, translation of AKT-1 mRNA was strongly inhibited by eS4–EGFP overexpression, whereas the accumulation of GRK2 and HRAS proteins was less affected.
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis of cells overexpressing eS4-EGFP.

claim: The accumulation of GRK2 and HRAS proteins was less affected by eS4–EGFP overexpression than AKT-1.
source: Notably, translation of AKT-1 mRNA was strongly inhibited by eS4–EGFP overexpression, whereas the accumulation of GRK2 and HRAS proteins was less affected.
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis of cells overexpressing eS4-EGFP.

claim: A slight increase in eIF4B protein level was observed upon transfection of eS4–EGFP.
source: A slight increase in eIF4B protein level was also observed upon transfection of eS4–EGFP (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis, shown in Figure 6d.

claim: ES6S blockage by both VIC–oligo 4 and eS4–EGFP resulted in comparable effects on translation.
source: This confirmed that ES6S blockage by both VIC–oligo 4 and eS4–EGFP resulted in comparable effects on translation.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of effects of the two blocking methods.

claim: The addition of VIC–oligo 4 to rabbit reticulocyte lysates (RRL) drastically inhibited the translation of mRNAs bearing stable RNA stem-loops in their 5′ UTRs.
source: As observed in transfected cells, the addition of VIC–oligo 4 to rabbit reticulocyte lysates (RRL) drastically inhibited the translation of mRNAs bearing stable RNA stem-loops in their 5′ UTRs.
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro translation experiments.

claim: For mRNAs with short and unstructured 5′ UTRs (63 nt and G-less), translation was unaffected or even stimulated by VIC–oligo 4 when reactions were measured at end-point times.
source: However, for mRNAs with short and unstructured 5′ UTRs (63 nt and G-less), translation was unaffected or even stimulated by VIC–oligo 4 when reactions were measured at end-point times (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro translation experiments, shown in Figure 7a.

claim: FITC–oligo 4 accelerated the accumulation of luc activity in the reactions programmed with 5′ UTR G-less mRNA, and to a lesser extent in those programmed with 5′UTR 63 mRNA.
source: Surprisingly, FITC–oligo 4 accelerated the accumulation of luc activity in the reactions programmed with 5′ UTR G-less mRNA, and to a lesser extent in those programmed with 5′UTR 63 mRNA (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a finding from real-time translation experiments, shown in Figure 7b.

claim: FITC–oligo 4 reduced the FTT of 5′ UTR G-less mRNA by 2 min, suggesting accelerated scanning.
source: FITC–oligo 4 reduced the FTT of 5′ UTR G-less mRNA by 2 min, suggesting accelerated scanning (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is a finding from full translation time analysis, shown in Figure 7c, with an inference about scanning speed.

claim: The addition of FITC–oligo 4 to 5′ UTR-SL20 mRNA drastically reduced the accumulation of luc activity at every time point, although the FTT was not significantly altered, suggesting arrest rather than delay of scanning.
source: In parallel experiments using highly structured 5′ UTR-SL20 mRNA, the addition of FITC–oligo 4 drastically reduced the accumulation of luc activity at every time point, although the FTT was not significantly altered, suggesting arrest rather than delay of scanning (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is a finding from real-time translation experiments, shown in Figure 7c, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Addition of hipp to 5′ UTR-SL20 mRNA delayed the accumulation of luc activity, which followed a differently shaped curve than that observed for FITC–oligo 4.
source: Interestingly, addition of hipp to 5′ UTR-SL20 mRNA delayed the accumulation of luc activity, which followed a differently shaped curve than that observed for FITC–oligo 4 (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a finding from real-time translation experiments, shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The addition of hipp increased the FTT by 2 min, suggesting a delay in the scanning process.
source: In contrast to the addition of FITC–oligo 4, the addition of hipp increased the FTT by 2 min, suggesting a delay in the scanning process.
evidence: This is a finding from full translation time analysis with an inference about scanning.

claim: The effect of eIF4A inhibition was similar but not identical to that observed for FITC–oligo 4 on mRNAs that have stable structures in their 5′ UTRs.
source: Thus, the effect of eIF4A inhibition was similar but not identical to that observed for FITC–oligo 4 on mRNAs that have stable structures in their 5′ UTRs.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparative kinetic data.

claim: The combination of VIC–oligo 4 and 0.3 μM hipp induced a dramatic synergistic inhibition of translation of 5′ UTR-SL30 mRNA (up to 60-fold).
source: Clearly, the combination of VIC–oligo 4 and 0.3 μM hipp induced a dramatic synergistic inhibition of translation of 5′ UTR-SL30 mRNA (up to 60-fold), whereas the effect on 5′ UTR-G41 translation was less dramatic (12-fold inhibition) (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is a finding from combination treatment experiments, shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The effect of combined VIC–oligo 4 and hipp on 5′ UTR-G41 translation was less dramatic (12-fold inhibition) than on 5′ UTR-SL30 mRNA.
source: Clearly, the combination of VIC–oligo 4 and 0.3 μM hipp induced a dramatic synergistic inhibition of translation of 5′ UTR-SL30 mRNA (up to 60-fold), whereas the effect on 5′ UTR-G41 translation was less dramatic (12-fold inhibition) (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is a finding from combination treatment experiments, shown in Figure 7d.

claim: These results strongly suggest that the function of eIF4A helicase and the ES6S region converge during the initiation step.
source: These results strongly suggest that the function of eIF4A helicase and the ES6S region converge during the initiation step.
evidence: This is an inference from the synergistic inhibition data.

claim: The topology of the ES6S region resembles an open channel rather than a narrow cleft like the decoding groove.
source: Rather than a narrow cleft like the decoding groove, the topology of the ES6S region resembles an open channel in which some differences in the accommodation of mRNA molecules are found.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural data and crosslinking results.

claim: The presumed flexibility of ES6S extensions, especially of ES6SA and ES6SB, may assist in the placement of mRNAs according to their secondary structure content.
source: The presumed flexibility of ES6S extensions, especially of ES6SA and ES6SB, may assist in the placement of mRNAs according to their secondary structure content.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural features and functional data.

claim: These extensions are similar to the tentacle-like structures described recently for some ESs of the 60S subunit, which are involved in the recruitment of MetAP and NatA proteins to 80S.
source: These extensions are similar to the tentacle-like structures described recently for some ESs of the 60S subunit, which are involved in the recruitment of MetAP and NatA proteins to 80S (Fujii et al., 2018; Knorr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: As eIF4G has been found to contact both ES6SE and ES6SB extensions, direct participation of eIF4F in the accommodation of the mRNA in the ES6S region seems likely.
source: Moreover, as eIF4G has been found to contact both ES6SE and ES6SB extensions (Yu et al., 2011), direct participation of eIF4F in the accommodation of the mRNA in the ES6S region seems likely.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous structural data, supported by a citation.

claim: The exact placement of the eIF4A helicase bound to mRNA in the scanning complex could not yet be mapped, most probably because of the dynamic nature of eIF4A–mRNA interactions.
source: Nonetheless, the exact placement of the eIF4A helicase bound to mRNA in the scanning complex could not yet be mapped, most probably because of the dynamic nature of eIF4A–mRNA interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study with a speculative explanation.

claim: Some mutations in the RNA-binding domain of eIF3g have shown decreased processivity of scanning of the structured 5′ UTRs of yeast mRNA.
source: Furthermore, some mutations in the RNA-binding domain of eIF3g have shown decreased processivity of scanning of the structured 5′ UTRs of yeast mRNA (Cuchalová et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a reference to previous literature.

claim: The possibility that other RNA helicases, such as DDX3, DHX9 and DHX36, could also associate with the ES6S region to unwind dsRNA and G4 structures in mRNA deserves further investigation.
source: The possibility that other RNA helicases, such as DDX3, DHX9 and DHX36, could also associate with the ES6S region to unwind dsRNA and G4 structures in mRNA deserves further investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: The blocking activity showed by oligo 4 was only observed when relatively bulky molecules (such as VIC) were conjugated to its 5′ extreme.
source: The blocking activity showed by oligo 4 was striking because it was only observed when relatively bulky molecules (such as VIC) were conjugated to its 5′ extreme.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: The fluorophores probably project toward the cavity of the ES6S region, at least partially blocking it.
source: Although the exact arrangement of VIC–oligo 4 bound to 40S was not determined, the fluorophores probably project toward the cavity of the ES6S region, at least partially blocking it.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on structural modeling.

claim: The binding of VIC–oligo 4 to the target sequence may restrict the conformational changes that ES6SA and ES6SB helices have been shown to undergo during initiation.
source: However, we cannot rule out the possibility that the binding of VIC–oligo 4 to the target sequence may also restrict the conformational changes that ES6SA and ES6SB helices have been shown to undergo during initiation (Melnikov et al., 2012; Toribio et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The differential sensitivity of mRNAs to the translational blockage imposed by VIC–oligo 4 reveals the existence of a great diversity in mRNA-dependence for scanning.
source: The differential sensitivity of mRNAs to the translational blockage imposed by VIC–oligo 4 reveals the existence of a great diversity in mRNA-dependence for scanning.
evidence: This is an inference from the genome-wide translation data.

claim: This differential effect can be explained if we consider the ES6S region as a true threading path for mRNA that makes the scanning of the 48S-PIC slower but more processive.
source: This differential effect can be explained if we consider the ES6S region as a true threading path for mRNA that makes the scanning of the 48S-PIC slower but more processive (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is a proposed model to explain the observed data, shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Translation initiation of mRNAs with short and unstructured 5′ UTRs could be enhanced by blocking of ES6S, as PIC recruitment and scanning of these mRNAs does not require unwinding.
source: Thus, translation initiation of mRNAs with short and unstructured 5′ UTRs could be enhanced by blocking of ES6S, as PIC recruitment and scanning of these mRNAs does not require unwinding.
evidence: This is an inference from the model and experimental data.

claim: Under ES6S blockage, mRNAs with short and unstructured 5′ UTRs could be threaded directly into the classical mRNA channel, bypassing the ES6S region and thus accelerating the scanning process.
source: Under ES6S blockage, these mRNAs could be threaded directly into the classical mRNA channel, bypassing the ES6S region and thus accelerating the scanning process (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism shown in Figure 8b, based on the model and data.

claim: These mRNAs with short and unstructured 5′ UTRs could also better compete for translational machinery in the context of general shut-off induced by VIC–oligo 4.
source: In addition, these mRNAs could also better compete for translational machinery in the context of general shut-off induced by VIC–oligo 4.
evidence: This is an additional inference to explain the observed upregulation of some mRNAs.

claim: Participation of the ES6S region in ribosomal attachment to mRNA would be dispensable, at least for some mRNAs with unstructured 5′ UTRs such as 5′ TOP mRNAs.
source: According to this, participation of the ES6S region in ribosomal attachment to mRNA would be dispensable, at least for some mRNAs with unstructured 5′ UTRs such as 5′ TOP mRNAs, which also show little or no requirement for eIF4A (Gandin et al., 2016; Meyuhas and Kahan, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 5′ TOP mRNAs show little or no requirement for eIF4A.
source: According to this, participation of the ES6S region in ribosomal attachment to mRNA would be dispensable, at least for some mRNAs with unstructured 5′ UTRs such as 5′ TOP mRNAs, which also show little or no requirement for eIF4A (Gandin et al., 2016; Meyuhas and Kahan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Whether mRNA is threaded into the ES6S region during ribosomal attachment, or rather is slotted into the ES6S region once the 5′-cap has entered the classical mRNA channel is still an open question that deserves further investigation.
source: However, whether mRNA is threaded into the ES6S region during ribosomal attachment, or rather is slotted into the ES6S region once the 5′-cap has entered the classical mRNA channel is still an open question that deserves further investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge and future research needs.

claim: For mRNAs that have long and structured 5′ UTRs, ES6S blockage probably reduces the processivity of the scanning complex along the 5′ UTR.
source: For mRNAs that have long and structured 5′ UTRs, ES6S blockage probably reduces the processivity of the scanning complex along the 5′ UTR.
evidence: This is an inference from the model and experimental data.

claim: The stem-loop and G4 structures in the 5′ UTR of mRNAs that are not effectively unwound in the ES6S region would become stacked at the mRNA entry channel, resulting in stalling and/or dissociation of the 48S-PIC from the mRNA.
source: The stem-loop and G4 structures in the 5′ UTR of mRNAs that are not effectively unwound in the ES6S region would become stacked at the mRNA entry channel, resulting in stalling and/or dissociation of the 48S-PIC from the mRNA.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the model.

claim: It is not clear whether 48S-PICs that bypass some stem-loops without unwinding would end up being productive.
source: Even if the 48S-PIC could bypass some stem-loops without unwinding, as previously observed in vitro (Abaeva et al., 2011), it is not clear whether these aberrant complexes would end up being productive.
evidence: This is a speculative statement with a citation to previous work.

claim: The DHX29 helicase located at the mRNA entry channel of PIC may alleviate the eventual stacking of some RNA structures at the mRNA entry channel.
source: The DHX29 helicase located at the mRNA entry channel of PIC may also alleviate the eventual stacking of some RNA structures at the mRNA entry channel (Hashem et al., 2013), although its involvement in the genome-wide unwinding of stable stem-loops and G4s is unknown.
